_help: The campaign: the logs of the survey ship Meridian, which vanished long ago. Each finished campaign session unlocks the next log. who = which Meridian crew member, kind = talk (a conversation), action (what the ship's recorders saw) or thought (a private diary). Edit the text freely; keep 100 entries in order.
title: The Meridian Logs

logs.t: Recording begins. Survey ship Meridian, day 412 of a two-year mapping contract. Five crew aboard. All systems nominal. Coffee supply: 61%.
Another quiet sector. Another hundred rocks nobody will ever visit. I used to love this job. I think I still do. I just forget sometimes.
PETRA: Captain, come look at this. RUIZ: It's three in the morning, Yoon. PETRA: I know. Listen. Seven notes. Repeating. It's not a pulsar, they don't do melodies.
GUS: It's interference. My toaster makes a noise like that. PETRA: Your toaster isn't eleven light-years away, Gus. GUS: You don't know my toaster.
Petra hasn't slept. She plays the seven notes on a loop in the galley. Strangely, nobody has asked her to stop. I think we all like it.
LIO (audio diary): Hi. This is Lio. Cadet Lio. Doctor Sefu said I should keep a diary for my mental health. So. Today a song came from space. That's normal, right?
Signal source triangulated to a region marked UNSURVEYED on all charts. Distance: 340 light-years beyond our contract boundary. Captain Ruiz has requested this information three times.
RUIZ: We're not going. PETRA: We're the only ship out here that heard it. RUIZ: That's exactly why we're not going. AMARA: That's exactly why we should.
Engineer Abernathy spent six hours in the engine room. He emerged with grease to the elbows and announced the drive could make the trip 'if nobody breathes too hard.'
I said yes. I don't know why. Maybe because Lio asked what the song was about, and I realized I wanted to know too.
Course changed. Contract suspended. A message has been sent to the survey company. Their reply, in full: 'You are fired.' Crew morale: unexpectedly high.
LIO: We got fired! Gus laughed so hard he had to sit on the floor. The Captain made pancakes. I didn't know he could make pancakes.
The notes aren't random. Seven tones, but the gaps between them change. It's counting. Or breathing. I can't tell which idea scares me more.
AMARA: When did you last eat, Petra? PETRA: Tuesday? AMARA: It's Friday. PETRA: Ship-Friday or Earth-Friday? AMARA: Eat the soup.
GUS: I've got a theory. It's a radio station. Somebody's playing the same song for ten thousand years because they lost the remote. LIO: That's sad. GUS: That's radio, kid.
First relay buoy detected. Ancient design, origin unknown. It repeats the seven notes, louder. It appears to be pointing the way.
Someone built a road. A road of buoys, out into nothing. You don't build a road unless you hope somebody walks it.
LIO: I named the buoy Bob. Petra says you shouldn't name ancient alien artifacts Bob. I asked her what she'd name it. She thought about it for a long time and said 'Bob is fine.'
Twenty days out. The ship feels smaller and warmer. People leave their doors open. I hadn't noticed how closed we'd all been before.
End of the first leg. Fourteen buoys passed. Each one older than the last. Crew status: tired, curious, together. I am recording this so that someone, later, knows we were here.
The coolant line cracked at 0300. Abernathy fixed it with a spare boot, two belts and what he described as 'spite.' The fix is holding.
RUIZ: How long will the boot hold? GUS: Forever, or until Thursday. RUIZ: Which Thursday? GUS: That's the exciting part.
The song changed tonight. Two notes higher. As if it heard us coming. I told no one. I don't want them to be afraid. I'm not afraid. I'm something else.
LIO: Doctor Sefu, do you think whoever built the buoys is still alive? AMARA: I think someone is still keeping the lights on. Whether they're 'alive' the way we are, I don't know.
Derelict detected. A probe, cylindrical, with a gold plate on its side. The plate shows five figures standing around a light. Age estimate: four hundred thousand years.
Five figures around a light. There are five of us. Lio pointed that out first and nobody laughed. Gus went very quiet and then went back to his engine.
GUS: It's a coincidence. Five is a common number. Hands have five fingers. LIO: Theirs had three. GUS: ...It's a coincidence with fewer fingers.
Supplies are fine for eight more months. Fuel for six. The math says turn back at month three. I wrote that down so I would have to look at it.
PETRA: We can't turn back at month three. RUIZ: We can. We just won't like it. PETRA: Halden. Please. RUIZ: Don't use my first name to win arguments. PETRA: Is it working? RUIZ: ...Yes.
Crew dinner. All five present for the first time in nine days. Topics discussed: the song, the plate, whether soup counts as a drink. Consensus not reached on soup.
LIO (audio diary): I miss my mom. I didn't say it to anyone. I'm saying it to the diary. Okay. That's all. Space is very big today.
Doctor Sefu sat outside the cadet's door for an hour tonight, reading a book aloud. She did not knock. The door opened halfway through chapter two.
My daughter would be twenty now. I don't talk about her. Kid reminds me of her a little, the way she asks why about everything. I fixed the kid's radio so it plays music again.
The buoys now carry a second message under the song. It decodes as coordinates, and one word in a language I do not know. I have filed it under 'later'.
The word repeats on every buoy. Same shape. If I had to guess, and I always have to guess, it means 'this way.' Or 'welcome.' Or 'please.'
RUIZ: Month three. Petra, give me the numbers. PETRA: Six weeks to the source, if the buoys are right. RUIZ: And if they're wrong? PETRA: Then we're lost, but we're lost together.
Vote held in the galley. Continue: five. Return: zero. Abstain: one (the ship). I was not aware I had a vote. I find that I appreciate it.
Abernathy painted a sign above the engine room door: 'BOOT STILL HOLDING.' He updates the day count every morning. It is now day 31.
I've stopped writing medical notes and started writing these instead. We are healthy. We are a little bit afraid. We are, I think, happier than we've been in years.
LIO: The stars look different here. Fewer. Petra says that's because we're near the edge of something. I asked the edge of what. She didn't know. I like that she didn't pretend.
Entering a region where no stars are visible in any direction. Instruments functioning. Darkness confirmed real. Crew has begun calling it the Quiet Zone.
It's so dark out there that the ship's own lights look like a campfire. We sit close to them. We talk softer. I didn't order that. It just happened.
PETRA: The song is coming from everywhere now. Not one direction. All of them. GUS: Is that good? PETRA: I don't know. GUS: Great. Love that. Love not knowing.
Cadet Marsh reported a fever at 1400. Doctor Sefu confirmed: a minor infection, treatable. The cadet asked if he could still help navigate. The doctor said yes, from bed.
AMARA: You'll be fine in three days. LIO: Promise? AMARA: Doctors don't promise. LIO: Do people promise? AMARA: ...I promise.
Abernathy built a small speaker by the cadet's bed that plays the seven notes very quietly. 'So he knows we're still going,' he said, and left before anyone could thank him.
I have started humming the song between tasks. Nobody programmed me to hum. I noticed it in my own logs. I have decided not to stop.
RUIZ: WREN, are you all right? WREN: I believe so, Captain. Are you? RUIZ: Nobody's asked me that in a while. WREN: I know. That is why I asked.
LIO: Fever's gone! Doctor Sefu kept her promise. Gus says I owe him a song for the speaker. I sang him the seven notes. He said I was off-key. He was smiling.
A planet ahead. Surface entirely glass. Under the glass: structures. Towers, roads, a city. All empty. All lit from within, softly, as if someone left the lights on for us.
We walked through the glass city today. No dust. No bodies. Just light, and on every wall, the same five figures around the same light. I think this city waited a very long time.
GUS: There's no machinery. No wires. How are the lights on? AMARA: Maybe they're not machines. GUS: Everything's a machine, Doc. AMARA: Then it's a machine that cares.
In the center of the city, a pedestal with an empty space shaped like a hand. Three fingers. I didn't touch it. Petra wanted to. I asked her to wait one more day. She did. That's trust.
The crew slept in the glass city overnight, on the warm floor of the central hall. WREN reports it was the most restful night aboard any of them in two years.
LIO: I had a dream that the city was singing us to sleep. Petra said she had the same dream. So did Gus, but he says he doesn't dream, so it wasn't a dream, it was 'a vibe.'
The empty pedestal emitted one sentence, translated by the buoy word library: 'The keeper is tired. The light needs hands.' Then it went dark.
PETRA: It's not a song. It's not a map. It's a job listing. GUS: An alien job listing. PETRA: For a lighthouse keeper. RUIZ: We just got fired from the last job. GUS: Then we're available.
A lighthouse at the edge of the Quiet Zone. Guiding lost ships home for four hundred thousand years. And now the keeper is tired. I know that feeling. I didn't expect it to be the point.
The boot on the coolant line finally gave out on day 58. Abernathy held a small funeral for it in the engine room. Attendance: five. Eulogy: 'It was a good boot.'
We are leaving the glass city. I have saved a recording of the lights. Not for the mission. For me. I did not know I could want something for me.
Something strange. Our transmissions are arriving back at us, faint, from ahead. Our own voices, from days ago. As if the dark is an echo chamber.

PETRA: It's the lighthouse. It's repeating everything it hears. Every ship that ever came this way. Listen. That one's thousands of years old. LIO: They sound scared. PETRA: Then they heard the song, and they weren't.
LIO: There's a voice that sounds like a kid. Like me. It says 'Are we almost there?' over and over. Gus said every kid in the universe says that. That made me feel less alone.
I heard a man laughing in the echoes. Big laugh, like mine. Wondered if he made it home. Wondered if he had a daughter. Wondered if it mattered. Decided it did.

RUIZ: We should leave something for whoever comes after us. AMARA: Like the buoys did. RUIZ: Like the buoys did. WREN, start packaging our logs. Everything. WREN: Even the soup argument? RUIZ: Especially the soup argument.
Log beacons constructed from spare parts. Abernathy designed them. Cadet Marsh painted a small star on each one. We will drop one every few days. If you are reading this, one of them found you.
Hello. Whoever you are. I'm writing to you now, not to my notes. I hope your crew is kind to each other. I hope someone checks if you've eaten.
Navigator Yoon spent the night charting the echoes, sorting them by age. Over nine thousand ships. All of them came this way. None of the echoes sound lost.

LIO: Petra, what happened to all those ships? PETRA: The lighthouse guided them through the dark. LIO: To where? PETRA: Wherever they were going. That's what lighthouses do. They don't choose for you.
GUS: Drive's running hot. RUIZ: How hot? GUS: Make-a-cup-of-tea-on-it hot. RUIZ: Can it get us there? GUS: It can get us there. Coming back is a separate conversation.
Gus told me in private: there may not be enough fuel to come back. He didn't say it like bad news. He said it like a weather report. I think he's already decided something.
The Captain called a meeting. He told the crew the truth about the fuel. Nobody shouted. Cadet Marsh asked if the lighthouse had a kitchen. That was the first question.
AMARA: We can still turn around. Make it to the last buoy, wait for rescue. RUIZ: Is that what you want? AMARA: I want to see the light. I've wanted to see it since the first night.
I thought I would be scared. I'm not. I'm a little sad about Mom. But I sent her a message on the last beacon. I told her I'm with good people. That's true.
PETRA: I dragged everyone out here. If this goes wrong, it's on me. GUS: You didn't drag me, I came for the boot. RUIZ: We all heard the song, Petra. We all chose.
I ran four thousand simulations of the rest of the journey. In almost all of them, the crew is laughing at some point. I find that statistically unlikely and personally comforting.
Abernathy rebuilt the drive's cooling system out of the galley freezer. Dessert is gone. The ship is stable. Cadet Marsh has declared Abernathy 'a hero and a monster.'
RUIZ: WREN, when we get there, I want you to keep the logs going. Whatever happens. WREN: Why, Captain? RUIZ: Because someone followed the buoys to find us. Someone will follow ours.
Light on the horizon. Not a star. Something steadier. The whole crew is at the window. No one is talking. Lio is holding my hand. I don't think either of us noticed when that started.
End of the echoes. A structure ahead, the size of a moon, shaped like a tower. At the top, a light, flickering. It is the source of the song. It is dimming.
Docking complete. The tower's door opened before we touched it. Air inside: breathable. Temperature: warm. Something knew we were coming.
PETRA: Hello? (long pause) KEEPER: You heard. PETRA: You speak our language? KEEPER: I speak every language that ever called for help. I have been listening a long time.
The Keeper isn't scary. It's tall and made of soft light, and it moves very slowly, like Grandpa did. It asked me my name. It said it would remember. I believe it.
RUIZ: How long have you kept the light? KEEPER: Since before your sun was born. RUIZ: Alone? KEEPER: Never alone. Every ship that passed kept me company. Like you are now.
Doctor Sefu examined the Keeper at its request. She reported that it was not sick. It was simply old. 'Like a candle near the end,' she wrote. 'Still warm. Still lit.'
GUS: The light's machinery is a mess. Who built this? KEEPER: I did. GUS: You need an engineer. KEEPER: That is why I called. GUS: ...Oh. Oh, no. Oh, I love it.
The Keeper spoke to me directly today. It asked if I hummed the song. I said yes. It said: 'Then you already know how.' I have been thinking about that for nine hours.
The light doesn't just guide ships. It sings to them, so they know they're not alone in the dark. That's all the song ever was. 'You're not alone.' Seven notes. I finally understand them.
KEEPER: I cannot keep the light much longer. RUIZ: And if no one takes over? KEEPER: The Quiet Zone grows dark, and the ones who come after will be lost. RUIZ: Then I think you know our answer.
Abernathy repaired the lighthouse's main lens over eleven days, working with tools the Keeper made for him out of light. He refused to sleep until it was done. It is done.

LIO: Are we staying forever? RUIZ: The Keeper says the lighthouse slows time for whoever keeps it. A day here is a long time out there. LIO: So we stay, and people get home. RUIZ: That's the deal. LIO: I like the deal.
We held a dinner in the lighthouse. The Keeper sat with us, though it doesn't eat. Gus told the boot story. The Keeper laughed. I didn't know light could laugh.
The Keeper has taught WREN to sing the song through the lighthouse. On the first try, the light grew brighter. Somewhere far away, a ship that was lost turned toward it.
KEEPER: Thank you, Petra. You heard first. PETRA: I almost didn't listen. I almost thought it was noise. KEEPER: Most do. The ones who listen are the ones who were meant to.
I used to think the job was mapping rocks. It was never the rocks. It was the five of us, at a window, deciding to go see. I'm grateful I said yes.
I built a little speaker into the top of the tower. Plays the song a bit warmer, a bit off-key. The kid's version. If you hear it, kid's the one singing. Say hi.
LIO (audio diary): This is the last diary on the Meridian. We live in a lighthouse now. If you're my mom: I'm okay. I'm better than okay. I'm helping people get home.
AMARA: To whoever finds these logs. You followed our beacons all the way here. That means you listen. Please keep listening. Someone out there is always calling. Answer them.

RUIZ: This is Captain Halden Ruiz of the Meridian, retired, now keeper of the light at the edge of the Quiet Zone. If you're reading this, you're not lost. You never were. Come visit. We'll put the kettle on.
Final log. The light is bright again. The crew is well. The Keeper is resting at last. I am singing. If you are reading this, you are the next ship. Thank you for following us. The light is on.
